analysis.one_liner: Forces old fossil-fuel power plants to run efficiently and cut mercury, carbon, acid rain, and smog pollution.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every fossil-fuel power plant to meet efficiency and pollution limits within ten years, closing the loophole that let plants built before the 1970 Clean Air Act run with far weaker controls. It set specific caps on mercury, carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, and nitrogen oxides, extended tax credits to solar and geothermal power, and funded worker retraining and economic help for coal communities. It also included tax breaks and research funding for coal plant owners who built cleaner, more efficient units.
analysis.who_benefits: People who breathe power plant pollution: the bill's findings cite fine particle pollution associated with roughly 50,000 American deaths a year, smog that worsens asthma, and mercury contamination that makes fish unsafe to eat, with the greatest risk to pregnant women and children [S3]. Consumers would also have received annual disclosure of the pollution from the plants generating their electricity [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living downwind of coal plants

how_it_helps.text: It closed the 'grandfather' loophole: within ten years, every fossil-fuel plant — regardless of when it was built — had to meet the same new source review requirements as new plants, a standard the bill says only 23% of the 1,000 largest emitting units then faced [S2][S3].

It set hard emission limits: 90% removal of mercury from coal and oil, 95% removal of sulfur dioxide, 90% removal of nitrogen oxides, and per-kilowatt-hour carbon dioxide caps by fuel type, with public reporting of each facility's emissions [S3].
It required plants to achieve at least 45% combustion efficiency — against an average of 33% at the time — forcing retirement of the oldest, least efficient units [S3].
It required plants to tell residential customers, at least annually, how much pollution the unit generating their power emits [S3].
It extended the renewable energy production tax credit to solar and geothermal power through 2016 and funded demonstrations of wind, biomass, fuel cells, and cleaner coal technologies [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of old, inefficient fossil-fuel plants would bear the cost of efficiency upgrades, pollution controls, and a 30-cent-per-megawatt-hour fee that funds the new Clean Air Trust Fund [S3]. Those costs would be expected to show up in electricity rates, and the bill itself provides transition aid for coal workers and communities on the assumption that coal use would fall [S3].

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden was steep: retrofitting plants to 45% efficiency with 90% mercury capture within ten years would require large capital spending, and owners could be expected to pass those costs to electricity customers [S3].

The bill does not simply regulate coal — it subsidizes it, funding a clean coal demonstration program at $75 million a year, accelerated tax depreciation for investor-owned plants, and grants to publicly owned utilities [S3].

It authorized $75 million a year in worker retraining and $75 million a year in community aid for coal-dependent regions, acknowledging that the standards would reduce coal consumption and cost some workers their jobs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case was strong and specific — mercury neurotoxicity, smog, acid rain, and fine particles the bill's findings link to tens of thousands of deaths a year — but the compliance costs were real and would have flowed through electricity bills, and the bill bought industry cooperation with coal subsidies and tax breaks that modestly weaken its environmental purpose. The design acknowledged the transition problem rather than ignoring it.

outcome.mechanism: It died in the Senate Finance Committee: introduced in June 2001 with no cosponsors, referred to Finance the same day, and never reported out or voted on before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Leahy introduced the bill on June 28, 2001, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance — its only action of the Congress [S1][S5].
The Finance Committee never scheduled consideration, and no further action appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of grandfathered coal and oil plants were better off: they avoided the efficiency mandates, emission caps, and per-megawatt-hour fee, and continued operating under the weaker pre-1970 rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners of old grandfathered coal plants

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor; the bill's sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in June 2001 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or report — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration.

against.name: Coal-fired electric utilities and coal producers
against.role: Regulated industry whose plants the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: The record shows no cosponsor stepped forward from either party in the two years the bill sat in the coal-producing state of Iowa's Finance Committee; no industry group lobbied for it on the record.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator from either party cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never appeared on the record.

industries.note: The bill's efficiency mandates, emission caps, and generation fee fell hardest on owners of old grandfathered coal plants, whose interest was in continuing to run under the pre-1970 rules. At the same time, the bill offered them clean coal research funding, accelerated depreciation, and customer-funded transition aid, so cleaner operators had a path to benefit.

The bill anticipated reduced coal consumption by power plants and provided $75 million a year each for coal worker retraining and coal community economic development — an acknowledgment that less coal would be burned.

The bill extended the production tax credit to solar and geothermal through 2016 and funded demonstration projects for wind, biomass, and fuel cells, expanding these industries' market as fossil units faced limits.

Gas plants faced the loosest carbon dioxide cap and easiest efficiency path, positioning them to gain share as coal units were forced to modernize, though gas units also had to meet the sulfur and nitrogen limits.
